screens.title: Implementing Database Maintenance Plans
screens.narratorSegment: In this short course you will learn to design and operate a maintenance plan that keeps Azure S Q L databases fast, reliable, and recoverable. Maintenance covers recurring tasks you run inside the database: managing index fragmentation and statistics so queries remain efficient, running integrity checks to detect corruption early, managing transaction logs to avoid full logs and failed transactions, and periodic cleanup to keep data size manageable. Azure handles much of the underlying platform, but database-level maintenance is your responsibility. You will see concrete T-S Q L commands used in production, a safe pattern for batching large deletes, and scheduling options for Managed Instance and Azure S Q L Database. Along the way we highlight common mistakes — for example, using shrink operations as a routine measure — and show safer alternatives. By the end of this lesson, you will recognize when to rebuild versus reorganize an index, how and when to update statistics, and how to incorporate jobs or automation so maintenance runs outside peak hours. Consider one simple question as you watch: if a query suddenly slows after a bulk import, which maintenance step would you check first and why?

screens.title: Why proactive database maintenance matters
screens.narratorSegment: Database maintenance is a set of recurring in-database tasks that preserve performance, data integrity, and recoverability. Although Azure manages the underlying platform for PaaS services, the contents and structure of your tables, indexes, and logs still belong to you. Neglecting maintenance can allow index fragmentation to increase, statistics to become stale, and transaction logs to grow unexpectedly. These conditions cause longer query times, more input and output, and in extreme cases, corruption that affects business continuity. A simple concrete example: after importing millions of rows into a table, the nonclustered index may become highly fragmented and the optimizer's statistics are out of date. Running an index rebuild with online option and updating statistics removes fragmentation and gives the optimizer accurate distribution information, often restoring query performance quickly. Common misconceptions include thinking that platform-managed backups or automatic checks remove the need for maintenance — they do not replace in-database tasks. Key takeaway: view maintenance as preventive care for your data, scheduled during off-peak windows and validated by job histories and metrics. Why proactive database maintenance matters means treat maintenance as preventive care: regular actions prevent degradation and keep query performance and recovery readiness predictable.. In practical terms, performance, integrity, and recoverability depend on regular in-database tasks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Why proactive maintenance matters
Definition and purpose

Maintenance covers index care, statistics updates, integrity checks, log and cleanup routines that together keep the database performant and recoverable.

Example: After a large import, the nonclustered index becomes fragmented and statistics are stale, causing a query plan regression.
Misconception: Platform-managed backups replace in-database maintenance. They do not; backups help recover, but they don't fix fragmentation or stale statistics.
Why it matters
Timely maintenance reduces I/O, lowers latency, and ensures that integrity checks and recovery are reliable when you need them.
Practical checklist
  • Measure fragmentation and set thresholds for rebuild versus reorganize.
  • Update statistics after major data changes or index rebuilds.
  • Schedule DBCC CHECKDB on Managed Instance or use automation for Azure SQL Database.
  • Plan log backups or automation to prevent log saturation on MI/VM.
Key Takeaway

Maintenance prevents slowdowns, protects recovery, and should be measured and scheduled as part of operations.

screens.title: Index Rebuild vs Index Reorganize
screens.narratorSegment: Index rebuild and reorganize both reduce fragmentation, but they differ in effect and impact. A rebuild drops and recreates the index, eliminating fragmentation completely, reclaiming space, and updating statistics. By default a rebuild can be offline and block access, although Azure S Q L Database, Managed Instance, and Enterprise Edition support an online rebuild option. Reorganize is an online, lighter-weight operation that physically reorders the leaf pages to improve contiguity without dropping the index. It consumes fewer resources and never blocks, but it is less effective for severe fragmentation and does not reclaim space as thoroughly. A practical rule: use reorganize for moderate fragmentation, for example between five and thirty percent, and rebuild when fragmentation exceeds roughly thirty percent or when you need to reclaim space. A common mistake is running frequent full rebuilds during peak hours; prefer online rebuilds in production when available, and schedule heavy operations during off-peak windows. Think of reorganize as tidying a bookshelf and rebuild as taking everything down and re-shelving it in order. Index Rebuild vs Index Reorganize means reorganize for moderate fragmentation and minimal disruption; rebuild for severe fragmentation or when reclaiming space and updating statistics is required.. In practical terms, when to use each operation and what they change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Index Rebuild vs Reorganize
Rebuild
Drops and recreates index, removes fragmentation, reclaims space, and updates statistics. Can be offline unless online option is supported.
When to rebuild: fragmentation > 30%, need to reclaim space, or after massive data churn.
Consideration: use WITH (ONLINE = ON) in supported Azure services to reduce downtime.
Reorganize
Physically reorders leaf-level pages to match logical order. Always online and less resource intensive, but less effective for severe fragmentation.
When to reorganize: fragmentation between about 5% and 30% when you want minimal disruption.
Trade-off: fewer resources and no blocking, but does not reclaim disk space as well as a rebuild.
Example
If sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats shows 40% fragmentation on a critical index, plan a rebuild with ONLINE = ON during off-peak hours to restore performance and update statistics.
Key Takeaway

Choose reorganize for light maintenance and rebuild for thorough correction; schedule heavy operations to limit user impact.

screens.title: Measuring fragmentation and choosing an action
screens.narratorSegment: A repeatable process helps you decide whether to reorganize, rebuild, or do nothing. Start by querying sys. dm_db_index_physical_stats for the target database, object, and index to obtain average fragmentation percentage. If fragmentation is low, typically below about five percent, no action is needed. If fragmentation is moderate, between roughly five and thirty percent, reorganize the index. If fragmentation is high, above approximately thirty percent, plan a rebuild and consider the ONLINE option for production workloads in Azure S Q L Database or Managed Instance. After any reorganize or rebuild, update statistics with a full scan to give the optimizer accurate distribution metrics. Schedule these checks on a cadence appropriate for the workload — busy OLTP systems will need more frequent checks than static reporting databases. A common misstep is failing to re-evaluate thresholds over time; monitor job effectiveness by comparing query performance and fragmentation before and after maintenance so you can tune the cadence and thresholds. Measuring fragmentation and choosing an action means measure fragmentation, apply thresholds (≤5% none, 5–30% reorganize, >30% rebuild), then update statistics and verify improvement.. In practical terms, a decision flow using sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Measuring fragmentation
Steps
  1. Run sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats for the database, object, and index.
  2. If fragmentation ≤ 5%: no maintenance required.
  3. If fragmentation > 5% and ≤ 30%: run ALTER INDEX REORGANIZE.
  4. If fragmentation > 30%: run ALTER INDEX REBUILD; use ONLINE = ON if supported.
  5. After maintenance: run UPDATE STATISTICS with FULLSCAN for accurate optimizer data.
Common mistake
Relying on a single run of maintenance without post-checks; always confirm fragmentation and plan metrics improved.
Concrete example
If sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats reports 35% fragmentation for IX_OrderDetails_ProductID, schedule ALTER INDEX REBUILD WITH (ONLINE = ON) during an off-peak window. After the rebuild, run UPDATE STATISTICS Sales.OrderDetails WITH FULLSCAN to refresh distribution metadata.
Key Takeaway

Use a measured decision flow and validate results; thresholds guide action but monitoring validates effectiveness.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Index maintenance T-SQL
T-SQL examples
Use these snippets as templates. Replace YourDatabaseName and object names with your targets and test carefully in a nonproduction environment.
USE YourDatabaseName;
GO

-- Rebuild a specific index online
ALTER INDEX IX_Customers_LastName_FirstName ON dbo.Customers REBUILD WITH (ONLINE = ON);
GO

-- Rebuild ALL indexes on a table online
ALTER INDEX ALL ON dbo.Customers REBUILD WITH (ONLINE = ON);
GO

-- Update statistics for a table with full scan
UPDATE STATISTICS dbo.Customers WITH FULLSCAN;
GO

-- Update statistics for a specific index
UPDATE STATISTICS dbo.Customers IX_Customers_LastName_FirstName WITH FULLSCAN;
GO
Concrete note
Always run UPDATE STATISTICS after rebuild if your workload needs the most accurate distribution data for plan selection.
Misconception
ONLINE = ON removes all risk; it reduces blocking but still consumes resources and must be scheduled with care.
Checklist before running
  • Verify disk and CPU headroom for heavy operations.
  • Schedule during low activity and notify stakeholders.
  • Capture job output and compare fragmentation before and after.
Key Takeaway

Use provided T-SQL templates, adapt names, run in test, and update statistics after maintenance to maximize optimizer benefit.

screens.title: Statistics and the Query Optimizer
screens.narratorSegment: Statistics are metadata that describe the distribution of values in one or more columns. The query optimizer uses statistics to estimate how many rows will match a predicate, which it calls cardinality. Accurate cardinality estimates lead the optimizer to choose cost-effective execution plans. If statistics are outdated after large data modifications, the optimizer can pick poor plans that cause excessive scans, improper join methods, or bad parallelism decisions. A practical example: after bulk-loading rows into a volatile table, a query that previously used an index seek might suddenly use a scan because the histogram the optimizer relies on is stale. The remedy is UPDATE STATISTICS with FULLSCAN for a complete refresh of distribution metrics, or use a sampled update when speed is essential and slight inaccuracy is acceptable. One common misconception is to over-rely on automatic statistics updates; auto-update is helpful but may not trigger immediately after massive changes. Key takeaway: keep statistics aligned with data volatility and schedule manual updates when needed. Statistics and the Query Optimizer means statistics inform the optimizer; keeping them current after large changes prevents poor plan choices and query regressions.. In practical terms, what statistics are and why updating them matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Statistics and the Query Optimizer
What are statistics?

Statistics are histograms and metadata about column value distribution used to estimate how many rows a query will return.

Concrete example
After bulk imports, the histogram may not reflect new value frequencies. The optimizer may choose a suboptimal plan until statistics are refreshed.
Tip: Use FULLSCAN when accurate distributions matter; use SAMPLE percent when you need speed.
Practical actions
  • Identify volatile tables and schedule more frequent statistic updates.
  • Run UPDATE STATISTICS TableName WITH FULLSCAN after big data loads or index rebuilds.
  • Monitor query plans for sudden cardinality estimate changes to signal stale statistics.
Key Takeaway

Accurate statistics are essential for the optimizer—refresh them after large data changes to prevent plan regressions.

screens.title: DBCC CHECKDB: integrity checks and scheduling
screens.narratorSegment: DBCC CHECKDB validates allocation and structural integrity across the database, detecting physical and logical corruption. For S Q L Server on VMs and Managed Instance, you can schedule DBCC CHECKDB as a S Q L Server Agent job and run it regularly — many teams run it weekly during low activity windows. Azure S Q L Database performs background integrity checks as part of the service, but you may still run DBCC CHECKDB or specific checks like DBCC CHECKTABLE after large data migrations or schema changes. For Azure S Q L Database, use Azure Automation runbooks or scheduled Azure Functions to invoke checks if you choose to run them manually. If CHECKDB reports errors, investigate immediately and consider restoring from the most recent clean backup; corruption can require a restore or more extensive repair steps. A misconception is to assume cloud-managed checks eliminate the need for any integrity validation; instead, combine platform checks with targeted runs after significant changes and keep a documented response plan for any detected corruption. DBCC CHECKDB: integrity checks and scheduling means run dbcc checkdb regularly where possible; for azure sql database, rely on platform checks and run manual checks after major operations using automation if needed.. In practical terms, how and where to run checks in azure sql environments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Batch cleanup
Batch delete pattern
Delete in chunks using a loop and a controlled batch size, then pause between batches to reduce lock duration and log pressure.
USE YourDatabaseName;
GO

DECLARE @RowsAffected INT = 1;
DECLARE @BatchSize INT = 10000;
DECLARE @CutoffDate DATETIME = DATEADD(year, -1, GETDATE());

WHILE @RowsAffected > 0
BEGIN
    DELETE TOP (@BatchSize) FROM AdminAuditLog
    WHERE ActionTimestamp < @CutoffDate;

    SET @RowsAffected = @@ROWCOUNT;

    IF @RowsAffected > 0
        WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01';
END;
GO
This pattern reduces transaction duration and gives the log time to be backed up and truncated between batches for MI/VM or managed operations in Azure SQL.
Checklist
  • Ensure the delete predicate has supporting indexes.
  • Start with small batch sizes and increase cautiously.
  • Monitor locks and log growth during the run.
Key Takeaway

Batched deletes are the safe way to remove large amounts of data while protecting availability and controlling log growth.

fullNarratorScript:
In this short course you will learn to design and operate a maintenance plan that keeps Azure S Q L databases fast, reliable, and recoverable. Maintenance covers recurring tasks you run inside the database: managing index fragmentation and statistics so queries remain efficient, running integrity checks to detect corruption early, managing transaction logs to avoid full logs and failed transactions, and periodic cleanup to keep data size manageable. Azure handles much of the underlying platform, but database-level maintenance is your responsibility. You will see concrete T-S Q L commands used in production, a safe pattern for batching large deletes, and scheduling options for Managed Instance and Azure S Q L Database. Along the way we highlight common mistakes — for example, using shrink operations as a routine measure — and show safer alternatives. By the end of this lesson, you will recognize when to rebuild versus reorganize an index, how and when to update statistics, and how to incorporate jobs or automation so maintenance runs outside peak hours. Consider one simple question as you watch: if a query suddenly slows after a bulk import, which maintenance step would you check first and why?

These objectives frame the practical skills you will practice. First, you'll learn why proactive maintenance matters: how regular tasks prevent slow queries, protect against data corruption, and reduce downtime. For example, you will interpret query plan regressions and link them to fragmentation or stale statistics. Second, you will write and run T-S Q L maintenance scripts that rebuild or reorganize indexes and update statistics efficiently; you'll see command examples and when to use full scans versus sampling. Third, you'll configure integrity checks with DBCC CHECKDB and choose appropriate scheduling mechanisms in Azure S Q L Managed Instance and Azure S Q L Database. We discuss what to do if a check reports errors. Fourth, you'll develop transaction log and cleanup strategies: how to manage log growth, schedule backups or automation, and implement batched deletions to avoid long running transactions and blocking. Each objective combines definition, a short hands-on pattern, and a verification milestone so you can confirm competency in your environment.

Now we clarify what success looks like when applying these objectives operationally. For index work, success means fragmentation levels are reduced on a schedule and query durations improve after maintenance. You will learn how to measure fragmentation with the dynamic management function and choose rebuild or reorganize based on thresholds. For statistics, success is the optimizer consistently producing efficient plans after major data changes, verified by plan stability and reduced scans. For integrity checks, success means running DBCC CHECKDB on a cadence suitable for your recovery objectives and reacting to any reported errors with investigation and restore strategies. For logs and cleanup, success is predictable log growth, regular backups or automation preventing full logs, and safely archived historical data so active data sets remain compact. Each objective is paired with a verification step so you can confirm competency in real environments without risking production availability.

Database maintenance is a set of recurring in-database tasks that preserve performance, data integrity, and recoverability. Although Azure manages the underlying platform for PaaS services, the contents and structure of your tables, indexes, and logs still belong to you. Neglecting maintenance can allow index fragmentation to increase, statistics to become stale, and transaction logs to grow unexpectedly. These conditions cause longer query times, more input and output, and in extreme cases, corruption that affects business continuity. A simple concrete example: after importing millions of rows into a table, the nonclustered index may become highly fragmented and the optimizer's statistics are out of date. Running an index rebuild with online option and updating statistics removes fragmentation and gives the optimizer accurate distribution information, often restoring query performance quickly. Common misconceptions include thinking that platform-managed backups or automatic checks remove the need for maintenance — they do not replace in-database tasks. Key takeaway: view maintenance as preventive care for your data, scheduled during off-peak windows and validated by job histories and metrics. Why proactive database maintenance matters means treat maintenance as preventive care: regular actions prevent degradation and keep query performance and recovery readiness predictable.. In practical terms, performance, integrity, and recoverability depend on regular in-database tasks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Index rebuild and reorganize both reduce fragmentation, but they differ in effect and impact. A rebuild drops and recreates the index, eliminating fragmentation completely, reclaiming space, and updating statistics. By default a rebuild can be offline and block access, although Azure S Q L Database, Managed Instance, and Enterprise Edition support an online rebuild option. Reorganize is an online, lighter-weight operation that physically reorders the leaf pages to improve contiguity without dropping the index. It consumes fewer resources and never blocks, but it is less effective for severe fragmentation and does not reclaim space as thoroughly. A practical rule: use reorganize for moderate fragmentation, for example between five and thirty percent, and rebuild when fragmentation exceeds roughly thirty percent or when you need to reclaim space. A common mistake is running frequent full rebuilds during peak hours; prefer online rebuilds in production when available, and schedule heavy operations during off-peak windows. Think of reorganize as tidying a bookshelf and rebuild as taking everything down and re-shelving it in order. Index Rebuild vs Index Reorganize means reorganize for moderate fragmentation and minimal disruption; rebuild for severe fragmentation or when reclaiming space and updating statistics is required.. In practical terms, when to use each operation and what they change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A repeatable process helps you decide whether to reorganize, rebuild, or do nothing. Start by querying sys. dm_db_index_physical_stats for the target database, object, and index to obtain average fragmentation percentage. If fragmentation is low, typically below about five percent, no action is needed. If fragmentation is moderate, between roughly five and thirty percent, reorganize the index. If fragmentation is high, above approximately thirty percent, plan a rebuild and consider the ONLINE option for production workloads in Azure S Q L Database or Managed Instance. After any reorganize or rebuild, update statistics with a full scan to give the optimizer accurate distribution metrics. Schedule these checks on a cadence appropriate for the workload — busy OLTP systems will need more frequent checks than static reporting databases. A common misstep is failing to re-evaluate thresholds over time; monitor job effectiveness by comparing query performance and fragmentation before and after maintenance so you can tune the cadence and thresholds. Measuring fragmentation and choosing an action means measure fragmentation, apply thresholds (≤5% none, 5–30% reorganize, >30% rebuild), then update statistics and verify improvement.. In practical terms, a decision flow using sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through practical T-S Q L you can adapt for your environment. The commands shown are the standard patterns used to rebuild a specific index, to rebuild all indexes on a table, and to update statistics with a full scan. Use ALTER INDEX... REBUILD WITH (ONLINE = ON) for production when the service supports online rebuilds to reduce blocking. After any index rebuild or reorganize, update statistics using UPDATE STATISTICS TableName WITH FULLSCAN to ensure the optimizer has current distribution data. The full-scan option reads every row and produces the most accurate statistics, which is valuable after bulk loads. In the examples I will show, replace the placeholder database and object names with your real names and test in a nonproduction environment first. Remember that PRINT statements and job history gives you visibility; capture and review those outputs to verify success. A common oversight is running UPDATE STATISTICS before an index rebuild; the correct order is perform the index operation, then update statistics if needed. Index maintenance and statistics: T-SQL examples means use online rebuilds where supported, then update statistics with full scan after index maintenance to ensure optimizer accuracy.. In practical terms, practical t-sql snippets to rebuild, reorganize, and update statistics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Statistics are metadata that describe the distribution of values in one or more columns. The query optimizer uses statistics to estimate how many rows will match a predicate, which it calls cardinality. Accurate cardinality estimates lead the optimizer to choose cost-effective execution plans. If statistics are outdated after large data modifications, the optimizer can pick poor plans that cause excessive scans, improper join methods, or bad parallelism decisions. A practical example: after bulk-loading rows into a volatile table, a query that previously used an index seek might suddenly use a scan because the histogram the optimizer relies on is stale. The remedy is UPDATE STATISTICS with FULLSCAN for a complete refresh of distribution metrics, or use a sampled update when speed is essential and slight inaccuracy is acceptable. One common misconception is to over-rely on automatic statistics updates; auto-update is helpful but may not trigger immediately after massive changes. Key takeaway: keep statistics aligned with data volatility and schedule manual updates when needed. Statistics and the Query Optimizer means statistics inform the optimizer; keeping them current after large changes prevents poor plan choices and query regressions.. In practical terms, what statistics are and why updating them matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception.
